young.html: Put your hand on your chest, or two fingers on the side of your neck. Feel the bump, bump, bump? That is your heart pushing blood. William Harvey was an English doctor who lived about 400 years ago. He asked a question nobody had answered well: where does all that blood go?

Back then, most doctors followed the old Greek doctor Galen. They thought the liver made new blood from food all the time, and the body used the blood up, like a fire burning wood. Harvey did some arithmetic. Every beat pushes out a little blood. Multiply by thousands of beats, and in half an hour the heart pushes out more blood than there is in the whole body. Nobody eats that much food! So the blood can't be made new and used up. It must go round and round, like water in a fountain's pump: out through the arteries, back through the veins.

young.name: gb-harvey
young.cap: Try Harvey's numbers. Even with small guesses, the heart pumps more than all the blood in the body in half an hour.

young.html: Count your own heartbeats. Sit quietly. Find your pulse at your wrist or neck, and count the beats for 15 seconds while a grown-up watches a clock. Multiply by 4 to get beats in a minute. Now jump up and down 20 times and count again. How many beats would that be in half an hour? (A grown-up's heart pushes out roughly a small juice box of blood each beat, about 70 milliliters.)
Harvey also looked at the little flaps inside veins, called valves. They work like one-way doors: blood can go toward the heart, but not back. That fit his idea perfectly.

full.html: William Harvey (1578–1657) studied medicine at Cambridge and then at Padua in Italy, the best medical school of the day, where his teacher Hieronymus Fabricius had described the little valves in the veins. Back in London he became a physician at St Bartholomew's Hospital and later physician to King James I and King Charles I. In 1628 he published a short Latin book in Frankfurt: An Anatomical Exercise on the Motion of the Heart and Blood in Animals, usually called De Motu Cordis.

For about 1,400 years doctors had learned the body from Galen of Pergamon. In Galen's picture, the liver turned food into dark blood, which seeped out through the veins and was used up as nourishment. Some blood passed through tiny pores in the wall between the heart's two sides and mixed with air to become bright "arterial" blood. The heart's main job was to make heat. Harvey had to overturn a picture taught in every university, using dissection, careful watching of living animals' hearts, simple experiments on people's arms, and a piece of arithmetic.

By watching the slow hearts of cold-blooded animals and dying animals, Harvey saw that the heart's important motion is the squeeze (systole), not the relaxing. When the heart squeezes, it hardens and pushes blood out into the arteries, and that push is the pulse you feel at your wrist. The heart is a muscle and a pump.

full.text: … I frequently and seriously bethought me, and long revolved in my mind, what might be the quantity of blood which was transmitted, in how short a time its passage might be effected, and the like … I began to think whether there might not be A MOTION, AS IT WERE, IN A CIRCLE. Now this I afterwards found to be true …
full.work: On the Motion of the Heart and Blood in Animals, chapter 8
full.author: William Harvey

full.html: In chapter 9 Harvey makes his estimate. He guesses low on purpose, so no one can say he exaggerated: the left ventricle holds about two ounces, and perhaps only a quarter or an eighth of it is pushed out at each beat.

full.text: Now in the course of half an hour, the heart will have made more than one thousand beats, in some as many as two, three, and even four thousand. Multiplying the number of drachms propelled by the number of pulses, we shall have either one thousand half ounces, or one thousand times three drachms, or a like proportional quantity of blood, according to the amount which we assume as propelled with each stroke of the heart, sent from this organ into the artery; a larger quantity in every case than is contained in the whole body!
full.work: On the Motion of the Heart and Blood in Animals, chapter 9
full.author: William Harvey

full.name: gb-harvey
full.cap: Change Harvey's guesses. However you set them, the pumped amount beats the body's whole supply. Switch to liters to see it in modern units.

full.html: Old apothecary units: 1 ounce = 8 drachms, and 1 pound = 12 ounces. So 1,000 beats of one drachm each is 1,000 ÷ 8 = 125 ounces, which is 10 pounds 5 ounces. Harvey gets exactly this figure in chapter 9.

full.title: Harvey's arithmetic
full.q: The ventricle holds 2 ounces and pushes out 1/4 of it each beat. The heart beats 1,000 times in half an hour. How much blood is pushed out, in pounds and ounces?
steps: In half an hour: 1,000 × ½ = 500 ounces.
That matches Harvey's own sum: "forty-one pounds and eight ounces".
full.a: 41 lb 8 oz, far more than the body holds.

full.title: With modern numbers
full.q: A resting adult's heart pushes out about 70 mL per beat at 70 beats a minute. The body holds about 5 liters of blood. How long does it take to pump the whole 5 liters?
full.a: About one minute: the whole supply goes round roughly once a minute at rest.

full.text: Idea 3: the experiments on the arm

full.html: Harvey's chapters 11 to 13 use a band tied around the upper arm, as doctors did for bleeding patients. A very tight band stops the arteries, which lie deep: the hand goes pale and cool, and the artery swells above the band, on the heart's side. A medium band squeezes only the veins near the surface: now the veins swell below the band and the hand fills with blood. So blood comes into the arm through the deep arteries and leaves through the veins. Pressing along a swollen vein shows the valves at work: you can push blood toward the heart, but not away from it.

full.text: The letters On the Circulation of the Blood

full.html: In 1649 Harvey published two open letters to Jean Riolan, a leading Paris anatomist who accepted only part of the idea: Riolan allowed some circulation through the large vessels but not through the whole body. Harvey answers calmly, adds new experiments, and asks his critics to look for themselves. His later work on how animals develop, On the Generation of Animals (1651), has its own rung on this ladder.

items: Harvey was not first to trace part of the path. The Arab physician Ibn al-Nafis, in Cairo in the 1200s, wrote that blood goes from the right side of the heart to the left through the lungs, not through pores in the heart's wall. Michael Servetus (1553) and Realdo Colombo (1559) described the same lung passage in Europe. Harvey's new step was the whole circle through the body, with proof.

He never saw the link between arteries and veins. Harvey reasoned that blood must pass from the smallest arteries to the smallest veins, but he had no microscope good enough to see how. Marcello Malpighi saw the capillaries in a frog's lung in 1661, four years after Harvey died.

He was not quickly believed. Many doctors, especially in Paris, resisted for decades. Harvey's friend John Aubrey wrote that his medical practice suffered after the book came out. Descartes praised the circulation in his Discourse on Method (1637) but argued, wrongly, that the heart moves by heating the blood.

full.text: What later science kept, and what it changed

full.html: Kept: the circulation, the heart as a muscular pump, one-way valves, and Harvey's way of arguing from measured quantities. Changed: Harvey still thought blood was "perfected" by the heart's heat and spirit; we now know the lungs add oxygen and remove carbon dioxide. The pace he guessed was far too slow: a resting heart sends the whole supply of blood round in about a minute, not half an hour, which makes his argument even stronger.

deep.html: Arithmetic as an argument. Harvey's chapter 9 is one of the first times a fact about living bodies was settled by an estimate. Notice how he argues: he chooses numbers smaller than the truth, so that a critic can't escape by saying the numbers are too big. If even the low estimate is impossible under the old theory, the old theory falls. Scientists still use this "conservative estimate" move today.

Authority and evidence. Harvey admired Aristotle and wrote respectfully of Galen. He says he learned anatomy "not from books but from dissections." Compare Galileo's Simplicio, who trusts Aristotle's words over a falling stone. How should we honor great teachers while correcting them?

Mechanism. Descartes and others took Harvey's pump as a sign that the body is a machine of pipes and valves. Harvey himself did not go so far; he still spoke of the blood's life and spirit. Whether a living thing is "just" a machine is a question the Great Books return to again and again.

Big questions. What makes a good estimate? When is it fair to reason past what you can see (as Harvey did with the capillaries)? Why might an old theory survive long after the evidence turns against it?

questions: Harvey picked low numbers on purpose. Why does that make his argument stronger, not weaker?
Harvey was sure blood passed from arteries to veins, but he couldn't see how. Was he right to believe it? When is it reasonable to believe something you can't see?
Galen's ideas lasted 1,400 years. What do you think made them so hard to replace?
Count your pulse before and after running. What changes, and why might your body need that?
Ibn al-Nafis, Servetus and Colombo each saw part of the picture before Harvey. Who should get credit for a discovery that many people helped make?
How do the one-way valves in veins help blood get back to the heart from your feet?
